This article has 21 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt indicates that 7xxx Al-Zn-Mg-Cu alloys can develop environmentally induced cracking in humid air through a time-dependent incubation process. Loading first concentrates stress in thin ligaments between pores, constituent particles, and the surface; creep, particle cracking, and pre-existing fissures can then create precursor damage. Humidity is particularly important when a sharp, tight fissure is present, because it provides a preferential site for condensation. Over several hours, enough microscale liquid water can accumulate to sustain corrosion, incorporating carbonate and bicarbonate species from atmospheric CO2 and producing a more aggressive confined chemistry. Reactive Mg-rich η-phase particles and Mg2Si particles are especially favorable initiation sites: they corrode readily, generate more hydrogen, and provide less effective barriers to hydrogen ingress than the alumina-covered aluminum matrix. Hydrogen charging and corrosion therefore assist crack initiation in highly stressed regions, although humid-air initiation sites are small and only lightly corroded compared with immersed SCC conditions. Surface condition strongly affects susceptibility: machining damage, near-surface deformation, residual stress, pores, and protective or smeared surface layers can either mask or promote initiation. Within the alloys studied, AA7449 and AA7085 showed nearly identical incubation times (58.70 versus 56.98 hours), suggesting that water condensation and development of local chemistry may dominate over differences in constituent-particle density. The excerpt does not establish a broad quantitative comparison of high-Zn alloys with all other aluminum alloy families.

## pqac-00000052

From text 'ludwig2022infraredspectroscopystudies pages 11-13'.

Bellamarie Ludwig and Taryn T. Burke. Infrared spectroscopy studies of aluminum oxide and metallic aluminum powders, part i: thermal dehydration and decomposition. Powders, 1:47-61, Mar 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/powders1010005, doi:10.3390/powders1010005. This article has 36 citations.

DRIFTS indicates that oxidized aluminum powder surfaces contain several chemically distinct hydroxyl environments, but their detectability depends strongly on hydration and oxide structure. Physically adsorbed water desorbs by roughly 100 °C; after this water is removed, surface hydroxyl bands become accessible. Reported bands include approximately 3730, 3700, 3670, and 3665 cm−1, assigned to bridged and tri-bridged hydroxyl structures. Artificially aged aluminum exposed to high temperature and relative humidity develops highly hydrated, trihydroxide-rich surface structures. With continued heating, the trihydroxide decreases or decomposes into a boehmite-like layer, while surface hydroxyl peaks emerge or change in relative prominence. The naturally aged aluminum showed the contrasting behavior: detectable surface hydroxyls were largely absent, suggesting that its oxide/hydroxide structure did not make hydroxyl groups accessible under the measurement conditions. The excerpt therefore supports a humid-aging pathway involving stronger hydration and trihydroxide formation, followed by boehmite-like decomposition during heating, whereas less-hydrated or naturally aged surfaces exhibit fewer observable hydroxyls. Bayerite is not explicitly identified in this excerpt; the relevant trihydroxide is discussed generically rather than assigned to a specific polymorph.


---

## pqac-00000053

From text 'ludwig2022infraredspectroscopystudies pages 8-11'.

Bellamarie Ludwig and Taryn T. Burke. Infrared spectroscopy studies of aluminum oxide and metallic aluminum powders, part i: thermal dehydration and decomposition. Powders, 1:47-61, Mar 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/powders1010005, doi:10.3390/powders1010005. This article has 36 citations.

DRIFTS/infrared spectroscopy tracks surface hydration through hydroxyl-region absorbances and their disappearance during heating. Naturally aged aluminum shows bands at 3655, 3620, 3548, and 3525 cm−1 assigned to bayerite, with additional bands at 3464 and 3437 cm−1 associated with reactive groups on gibbsite; this indicates a mixture of aluminum trihydroxide phases. Heating to 300 °C removes these trihydroxide bands and leaves no detectable hydroxyl content in the naturally aged sample. The highly humid/thermal-aged sample (AA-Al, aged at high relative humidity and 85 °C) develops extensive platelet, needle, rod, and pyramidal surface structures and additional hydroxide-region bands. On heating, its trihydroxide signals decline, while boehmite bands near 3100 and 3300 cm−1 persist; new isolated surface hydroxyl bands appear at 3670 and 3730 cm−1. Water immersion produces boehmite-like nanoplates or needles alongside some trihydroxide. After heating above 100 °C, boehmite modes become distinct, and trihydroxide falls below detection by 200 °C, likely converting to or being masked by boehmite. The excerpt provides limited direct comparison with deliberately dry aging, but indicates that humid or water exposure promotes hydrated trihydroxide formation, whereas dehydration favors boehmite/residual oxide surface character.

From text 'ludwig2022infraredspectroscopystudies pages 1-2'.

Bellamarie Ludwig and Taryn T. Burke. Infrared spectroscopy studies of aluminum oxide and metallic aluminum powders, part i: thermal dehydration and decomposition. Powders, 1:47-61, Mar 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/powders1010005, doi:10.3390/powders1010005. This article has 36 citations.

The excerpt indicates that DRIFTS/infrared spectroscopy distinguishes physically adsorbed water from chemically bound surface hydroxyls on oxidized aluminum and alumina powders. Heating removes physisorbed water, exposing hydroxyl-related absorption features. A bridged hydroxyl band near 3670 cm−1 occurs in alpha-, gamma-, and boehmite aluminas, while additional hydroxyl populations depend on the aluminum oxidation state, surface coordination, crystalline phase, and aging history. Atmospheric moisture makes aluminum and alumina powders hygroscopic: water accumulates physically on the surface and can also generate chemisorbed hydroxyl groups. Aging changes the oxide/hydroxide layer and depends on storage or preprocessing conditions. Naturally aged aluminum with extensive oxidation to a trihydroxide phase decomposes during heating and, according to the abstract, does not retain detectable surface hydroxyl peaks. Artificially aged powder behaves differently, retaining a boehmite-like surface and showing surface hydroxyl bands at approximately 3670, 3700, and 3730 cm−1. The excerpt does not provide a detailed direct comparison of explicitly humid versus dry aging conditions, nor does it fully quantify the relative formation of boehmite, bayerite, and trihydroxide under each condition. It does establish that water exposure, age, and thermal treatment control the oxide/hydroxide phase and hydroxyl signature.

The excerpt indicates that infrared spectroscopy distinguishes molecular water and surface hydroxyl species on alumina and oxidized aluminum surfaces. Heating removes physisorbed molecular water, reducing the broad hydroxyl/water band near 3500 cm−1 and revealing sharper surface-OH bands. For γ-alumina, bands near 3760, 3720, and 3670 cm−1 are associated with bridged hydroxyls, a debated water or hydroxyl site, and fully surface hydroxylated groups, respectively. α-alumina shows bands near 3775, 3710, and 3670 cm−1, while boehmite is distinguished by a sharp 3665 cm−1 band assigned to bulk bridge hydroxyls. The excerpt indicates that DRIFTS can distinguish aluminum-oxide and hydroxyl species through their characteristic infrared absorbance bands and can follow changes during heating. For boehmite, bulk layered hydroxyls occur near 3290 and 3096 cm−1, while dehydration changes, broadens, and attenuates the hydroxyl region as physisorbed water is removed. Heating also exposes surface hydroxyl bands near 3730, 3700, and 3665 cm−1, assigned to bridged and tri-bridged hydroxyls. In γ-alumina, the broad feature around 3500 cm−1 decreases upon heating because molecular water is lost, making surface hydroxyl peaks more visible. Thus, infrared spectroscopy separates adsorbed water from structurally bound or surface OH groups and tracks dehydration or phase-related changes. The excerpt describes three aluminum-powder histories—ten-year ambient aging, accelerated aging at 85 °C/85% relative humidity, and immersion in hot water—but does not provide the comparative spectral results needed to determine how dry versus humid aging changes the oxide layer or the relative amounts of boehmite, bayerite, and other trihydroxide phases. It only establishes that humid and water treatments were used to investigate such surface transformations, with water immersion conditions associated with boehmite-film preparation.

Aging history strongly affects the layer thickness: freshly ball-milled Al–NaCl powder, examined within about 30 minutes, had the thinnest oxide film, whereas washed-out aluminum exposed to water for approximately three hours and then air-dried for several days had the thickest. The reported thickness estimates were roughly 1.6–4.8 nm for freshly ball-milled Al–NaCl, 3.2–9.6 nm for as-received Al, and 4.6–13.8 nm for washed-out Al. The authors attribute this difference to faster or more extensive oxide growth in wet environments. function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table comparing the two storage conditions and their expected effect on powder degradation. Columns: Parameter, Room condition (~22°C, 55% RH, dew point ~13°C), Enclosure condition (~25°C, 35% RH, dew point ~9°C), Effect on powder degradation.

Rows:
1. Temperature: 22°C vs 25°C, +3°C accelerates kinetics slightly
2. Relative humidity: 55% vs 35%, large decrease; fewer water monolayers on surface
3. Dew point / absolute humidity: ~13°C (11 g/m³) vs ~9°C (8.5 g/m³), moderate decrease but less important than RH for adsorption
4. Water layers on flat Al2O3 (Deng 2008): ~3 layers vs ~1.5-2 layers, ~40-50% reduction in adsorbed water
5. Water monolayers on real Al (Graedel): ~13 vs ~10-12, moderate reduction
6. Ion diffusivity in water film (Scher 2023): moderate, very slow; both well below bulk water
7. Critical RH for atmospheric corrosion: ~70%, both conditions well below threshold
8. Arrhenius factor at Ea=71 kJ/mol: rate ratio exp[(Ea/R)(1/295-1/298)] ≈ 1.10, ~10% increase due to T
9. Arrhenius factor at Ea=150 kJ/mol: rate ratio ≈ 1.22, ~22% increase due to T
10. Net effect on adsorbed water: Decrease dominates; RH drop from 55→35% reduces water coverage by ~30-50%
11. Net effect on oxidation/hydration: Decrease; both conditions below critical RH, but lower RH further suppresses water-mediated reactions
12. Overall verdict: Enclosure is better for powder storage despite higher temperature

Title: "Comparison of Storage Conditions and Predicted Degradation Effects""}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Parameter | Room condition (~22°C, 55% RH, dew point ~13°C) | Enclosure condition (~25°C, 35% RH, dew point ~9°C) | Expected effect on powder degradation |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Temperature | ~22°C (295.15 K) | ~25°C (298.15 K) | A +3°C change modestly-to-moderately accelerates thermally activated steps; it does not increase equilibrium water coverage at fixed RH. |
| Relative humidity / water activity | ~55% | ~35% | Large beneficial decrease in the controlling equilibrium variable for surface adsorption; fewer molecular-water layers and less mobile interfacial water. |
| Dew point / absolute humidity | ~13°C; approximately 11.3 g H₂O/m³ | ~9°C; approximately 8.8 g H₂O/m³ | Approximately 22% less vapor per unit air volume. This reduces the water reservoir and drying load, although equilibrium adsorption is governed primarily by RH at the powder-surface temperature. |
| Water layers on flat Al₂O₃ | Approximately 3 molecular layers | Approximately 1.5–2 layers | Approximately 35–50% lower molecular-water coverage in the enclosure (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). |
| Water coverage on a real, microporous Al surface | Approximately 13 monolayer-equivalents | Approximately 10–12 monolayer-equivalents | Moderate reduction; the larger values than for flat Al₂O₃ include micropore/capillary water and are approximate readings from the published figure (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000046). |
| Al-ion mobility in the adsorbed water film | Low; still strongly confined relative to bulk water | Very low; at approximately 30% RH, modeled Al-ion diffusion is more than two orders of magnitude slower than bulk-water self-diffusion | Lower RH suppresses water-mediated ion transport and therefore corrosion kinetics; no measured 35%:55% rate ratio is available (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000042). |
| Practical corrosion-onset RH for clean Al | Below the reported ~70% onset | Further below the reported ~70% onset | Both are below the approximate onset reported for pristine indoor aluminum, but this is not a universal threshold: salts, defects, Mg/Li-rich phases, and crevices can permit localized reaction below 70% RH (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). |
| Arrhenius temperature factor, *E*ₐ = 71 kJ/mol | Baseline = 1.00 | `exp[(71000/R)(1/295.15 − 1/298.15)] ≈ 1.34` | Approximately 34% faster at 25°C—not 10%—if a simple Arrhenius law with this activation energy applies (pqac-00000035). |
| Arrhenius temperature factor, *E*ₐ = 150 kJ/mol | Baseline = 1.00 | `exp[(150000/R)(1/295.15 − 1/298.15)] ≈ 1.85` | Approximately 85% faster—not 22%—under that high-*E*ₐ assumption; low-temperature Cabrera–Mott oxide growth is field-assisted, so a single Arrhenius factor is only a sensitivity bound (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). |
| Net effect on adsorbed water | Higher | Lower | RH reduction dominates equilibrium uptake: flat-Al₂O₃ coverage is predicted to fall by roughly 35–50%, with a smaller but still favorable decrease on rough/microporous native oxide. |
| Net effect on oxidation, hydration, and H₂-producing reactions | Higher water activity and thicker adsorbed film | Slightly faster intrinsic kinetics but substantially lower water activity and mobility | Expected net decrease in water-mediated degradation. The conclusion is strongest for clean, passivated Al/AlSi10Mg and weaker for contaminated, damaged, Li-bearing, or highly Mg/Zn-enriched powders. |
| Overall verdict | Cooler but wetter | Warmer but drier | **The enclosure is preferable**, provided containers remain sealed and the enclosure RH is reliably maintained near 30–40%; the RH decrease should outweigh the +3°C temperature increase for weeks-to-months storage. |


*Table: Comparison of the lab room and dehumidified enclosure, including corrected Arrhenius temperature factors and humidity-dependent surface-water estimates. It shows why the lower enclosure RH is expected to outweigh its modest temperature increase for passivated powder storage.*

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table summarizing the sensitivity of different powder types (in the user's collection) to the storage condition change. Columns: Powder type, Primary surface phase, Sensitivity to RH change (55→35%), Sensitivity to T change (22→25°C), Net effect of enclosure, Key concern, Key references.

Rows:

Gas-atomized AlSi10Mg (15-45 μm): Native amorphous Al₂O₃ + MgAl₂O₄ spinel; High - reduces water layers by ~35-50%; Low - Ea-dependent but small; Net beneficial; Mg enrichment in oxide promotes oxidation at high RH, reduced water mitigates this; Raza 2021 doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2020.109358, Fedina 2022 doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024

function.name: create_artifact

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:

        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context: our lab in Provo, Utah (about 1,400 m elevation) makes and stores aluminum-alloy powders for additive-manufacturing research. A walk-in enclosure inside the lab is supplied with air from a refrigerant (compressor) dehumidifier and exhausted continuously to building exhaust. The surrounding room sits at 21.7-22.2 C and 35-60% relative humidity (RH), dew point 6-13 C, tracking outdoor humidity. On the first night with the dehumidifier on, air inside the enclosure was 24 C at 35-42% RH (dew point 8-10 C) while the room was expected at about 22 C and 56% RH (dew point about 13 C); a hand-held reading showed about 27 C (80 F) at about 30% RH. So the compressor heat raises the enclosure temperature by roughly 2-5 C while the dehumidifier removes about 15-30% of the water vapor. Powders stored there, in sealed containers with silica-gel packets inside chemical storage cabinets, include gas-atomized AlSi10Mg (15-45 um, from MSE Supplies), silicon powder (98-99.5% Si), stainless-steel powder, and soon ultrasonically atomized aluminum alloys containing Mg, Cu, Zn, Li, Sc, Zr, Ce and Er, made in an argon-purged atomizer (AMAZEMET rePowder). Question: will the warmer but drier enclosure air increase or decrease water uptake and oxidation of these powders during weeks to months of storage, compared with the cooler, more humid room? Specifically: (1) For aluminum and Al-Si-Mg powders with a native oxide, is the amount of adsorbed water governed mainly by relative humidity (water activity) or by absolute humidity / dew point, and how does it change with temperature at fixed RH? Give adsorption isotherm data (e.g., mg water per m2, or number of monolayers, versus RH) for aluminum, Al2O3 or native-oxide surfaces, silicon and AlSi10Mg where available. (2) What are the measured rates, rate laws and activation energies for near-ambient (15-50 C) oxide thickening, hydroxide formation (boehmite, bayerite, gibbsite) and hydrogen evolution on aluminum and Al-alloy powders as a function of RH? Is there a critical RH below which hydration is negligible? Using those numbers, estimate how much faster these processes run at 24-27 C than at 22 C, and whether that is outweighed by the drop from about 50-60% RH to about 30-40% RH. (3) Which alloying elements make aluminum powders more sensitive to humid storage (for example Mg surface enrichment in AlSi10Mg, Li in Al-Cu-Li alloys, Zn, Ce, Sc), and does stainless-steel or silicon powder care about a 2-5 C change at all? Give quantitative values with DOIs, and say explicitly where evidence is lacking or where results conflict.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this multi-part question about water adsorption, oxidation kinetics, and alloying effects on metal powders during storage.

Abstract:
Interaction between the water adsorption ability of aluminium-oxide-based sorbents and their chemical composition, acid-base properties of the surface, and textural characteristics has been analysed. Alumina desiccants were synthesized with the centrifugal–thermal activation of gibbsite followed by the hydration of the gibbsite under mild conditions. It was demonstrated that the multicyclic adsorption regeneration of samples under realistic conditions results in structural transformations and changes in the acidity of their surfaces and water adsorption ability. The modification of pseudoboehmite with alkali ions increases surface basicity and the dynamic capacity of adsorbents relating to water vapours. Equations have been presented that describe the adsorption and desorption processes taking place during water vapour adsorption with the materials studied.

In the present study, the oxidation mechanism of AlN is investigated through microstructure observation. The analysis indicates that the oxide layer is full of small pores. The formation of pores generates additional surface area to induce further reaction. The reaction thus controls the oxidation in the temperature range from 1050 to 1350 °C. The oxidation rate becomes slow as the oxide layer reaches a critical thickness.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Triply periodic minimal surfaces (TPMS) are mathematically defined minimal surfaces that exhibit zero mean curvature and repeat periodically along all three Cartesian axes. They integrate mathematically defined geometry with extensive functional adjustability. Their smooth, non-self-intersecting topology enables systematic control over relative density and improves load transfer efficiency within the lattice. Their large surface area-to-volume ratios further enhance specific energy absorption (SEA) and enable diverse functional uses. Recent developments in additive manufacturing (AM) have made it easier to create TPMS structures. As a result, they are now considered as the architected materials that combine biological, thermal, and mechanical functions within a single framework. This study presents a comprehensive overview of the major TPMS structures. It further highlights several AM techniques used for their fabrication and provides a critical evaluation of how geometric design, relative density, and post-processing influence their mechanical and thermal performances. This work also discusses recent developments in graded and hybrid TPMS structures. It further identifies the main challenges and future research directions related to multi-material additive manufacturing and data-driven topology optimization.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This work presents an experimental workflow coupled with statistical tools to optimize L-DED processing parameters to build defect-free AlSi10Mg multilayer parts. Experimental steps included the quantitative evaluation of single beads, single layers, and multilayers to define L-DED processing windows. Regression and desirability functions, together with multi-objective Bayesian optimization, were used to optimize the main L-DED process parameters to meet target single-layer features. The systematic collection of reliable experimental data was critical to the success of the optimization models, and a detailed methodology is provided. The proposed workflow enabled the production of crack- and macroporosity-free multilayer parts with high geometrical accuracy and metallurgical bond integrity, achieving densities from 99.55% to 99.80% and deposition efficiencies between 87 and 97%, significantly exceeding previously reported values. This work provides practical guidelines to evaluate the outcomes of the AM L-DED process and obtain multilayer AlSi10Mg parts free from deleterious defects.</jats:p>

## 1. Infrared Spectroscopy Studies of Aluminum Oxide and Metallic Aluminum Powders, Part I: Thermal Dehydration and Decomposition

    author = "Ludwig, Bellamarie and Burke, Taryn T.",
    title = "Infrared Spectroscopy Studies of Aluminum Oxide and Metallic Aluminum Powders, Part I: Thermal Dehydration and Decomposition",
    year = "2022",

    volume = "1",

    url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/powders1010005",
    publisher = "MDPI AG",
    issue = "1",
    issn = "2674-0516"
}


Abstract:
In this work, we study three aluminum oxides (alpha, gamma, boehmite) and various oxidized metallic aluminum powders to observe their dehydration and decomposition behavior using in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). We find that a temperature increase to the aluminum oxides (aluminas) reduces physically adsorbed water molecules to reveal the presence of hydroxyl groups. All three aluminas contained bridged hydroxyls located at 3670 cm−1; we found additional surface hydroxyls, which varied based on the oxidation state of the aluminum atom. Oxidized metallic aluminum powders that were aged resulted in similar behavior; however, the results differed depending on the method of aging. We find that naturally aged aluminum (NA-Al) powders with heavy oxidation in the form of the tri-hydroxide decomposed and did not reveal any detectable surface hydroxyl peaks. When aged using artificial methods (AA-Al), we find both surface hydroxyls, including bridged hydroxyls at 3670, 3700, and 3730 cm−1, and a remaining boehmite-like surface. These results show that metallic aluminum powders can be tailored for specific applications, regardless of age. It also elucidates different ways to pre-process the powders to control the surface oxide layer, corroborated by comparison with the models oxides studied herein.

Abstract:
The development of fortified healthy pleasant foods, in which saturated fats are replaced with unsaturated ones, poses a challenge for the food industry due to their susceptibility to oxidative rancidity, which decreases product shelf-life, causes the destruction of health-promoting molecules, and forms potentially toxic compounds. A comparative study applying the Arrhenius model was carried out to investigate the oxidative stability and predict the shelf-life of a newly developed no added sugar chocolate spread formulated with sunflower oil, and fortified with vitamin D, Mg, and Ca checked against two commercially available spreads: No Palm and a well-known commercially available product (RB). The results obtained from the accelerated shelf-life testing for peroxide value (PV) showed relatively higher activation energy (Ea, 14.48 kJ/mol K) for RB, whereas lower Ea (11.31–12.78 kJ/mol K) was obtained for No Palm and all the experimental spread chocolates. Q10 values were comparable (1.202–1.154), indicating a similar catalytic effect of the temperature upon the oxidation rate across all the investigated samples. The positive Gibbs free energies ranged from 75.014 to 83.550 kJ/mol and pointed out that the lipid oxidation reaction in the chocolate spread was an endergonic process. The predicted shelf-life at 293.15 K was 8.57 months (RB), 7 months (No Palm), and 6.8 months for all the experimental spreadable chocolate. However, the higher production of hydroperoxides was observed in chocolate fortified with magnesium-calcium carbonate nanoparticles and stored at 313.15 and 323.15 K, suggesting these particles may enhance lipid oxidation.

Abstract:
The surface film on pure magnesium and two aluminium-containing magnesium alloys was characterised after 96 h at 95% RH and 22 °C. The concentration of CO2 was carefully controlled to be either 0 or 400 ppm. The exposed samples were investigated using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscopy. The results showed that when the alloys were exposed to the CO2-containing environment, aluminium cations (Al3+) was incorporated into a layered surface film comprising a partially “hydrated” MgO layer followed by Mg(OH)2, and magnesium hydroxy carbonates. The results indicated that aluminium-containing magnesium alloys exhibited considerably less localised corrosion in humid air than pure magnesium. Localised corrosion in the materials under investigation was attributed to film thinning by a dissolution/precipitation mechanism.

Abstract:
Magnesium-based materials are used primarily in developing lightweight structures owing to their lower density. Further, being biocompatible they offer potential for use as bioresorbable materials for degradable bone replacement implants. The design and manufacture of complex shaped components made of magnesium with good quality are in high demand in the automotive, aerospace, and biomedical areas. Selective laser melting (SLM) is becoming a powerful additive manufacturing technology, enabling the manufacture of customized, complex metallic designs. This article reviews the recent progress in the SLM of magnesium based materials. Effects of SLM process parameters and powder properties on the processing and densification of the magnesium alloys are discussed in detail. The microstructure and metallurgical defects encountered in the SLM processed parts are described. Applications of SLM for potential biomedical applications in magnesium alloys are also addressed. Finally, the paper summarizes the findings from this review together with some proposed future challenges for advancing the knowledge in the SLM processing of magnesium alloy powders.

Abstract:
The most widely used metal additive manufacturing processes utilize powder that is spread or fed onto a building platform. Although there are reviews of the literature on some aspects of the powder, many aspects have been un-der-reviewed or unreviewed. The present work is a review of the literature on these aspects. The aspects reviewed were emerging methods of powder production, methods used to improve the quality of a powder after production by a well-established method, influence of variables of well-established powder production methods on powder properties, influence of powder production method on powder properties, and influence of powder reuse on properties of powders of a wide collection of alloys. A new method to assess the quality of additive manufacturing (AM) metal powders using the triboelectric charging concept is demonstrated using CpTi, Ti6Al4V, AlSi10Mg, IN 738, and SS 316L powders. Abstract:
The fabrication of high purity copper using additive manufacturing has proven difficult because of oxidation of the powder feedstock. Here, we present work on the hydrogen heat treatment of copper powders for electron beam powder bed fusion (EB-PBF), in order to enable the fabrication of high purity copper components for applications such as accelerator components and vacuum electronic devices. Copper powder with varying initial oxygen contents were hydrogen heat-treated and characterized for their chemistry, morphology, and microstructure. Higher initial oxygen content powders were found to not only reduce surface oxides, but also reduce oxides along the grain boundaries and form trapped H2O vapor inside the particles. The trapped H2O vapor was verified by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and residual gas analysis (RGA) while melting. The mechanism of the H2O vapor escaping the particles was determined by in-situ SEM heated stage experiments, where the particles were observed to crack along the grain boundaries. To determine the effect of the EB-PBF processing on the H2O vapor, the thermal simulation and the validation of single melt track width wafers were conducted along with melting single layer discs for chemistry analysis. A high speed video of the EB-PBF melting was performed in order to determine the effect of the trapped H2O vapor on the melt pool. Finally, solid samples were fabricated from hydrogen-treated copper powder, where the final oxygen content measured ~50 wt. ppm, with a minimal residue hydrogen content, indicating the complete removal of trapped H2O vapor from the solid parts.

The excerpt provides a relative-humidity adsorption isotherm for Al2O3, but not a direct conversion to mg/m2 and not data for metallic aluminum surfaces. On defective Al2O3, water initially dissociates at oxygen-vacancy sites, producing hydroxyl groups; hydroxyl coverage saturates rapidly at approximately 1% RH. Molecular water adsorption then proceeds with increasing RH. The reported film thickness is approximately one water layer (3 Å) at 15% RH, two layers (6 Å) at 35–40% RH, and four layers by 70% RH. Above 70% RH, the film grows rapidly, reaching approximately 18 Å, or six layers, at 90% RH. Earlier in the excerpt, the second, third, and fourth layers are stated to complete at approximately 40%, 55%, and 70% RH, respectively. Thus, the isotherm is strongly nonlinear: rapid initial hydroxyl formation at low RH, followed by molecular-water multilayer growth and a steep increase above roughly 70% RH. The supplied passage frames adsorption primarily in terms of RH, effectively water activity at the surface, rather than absolute humidity. It also cautions that RH should account for surface temperature because desorption depends exponentially on surface temperature; the error from using surface temperature is stated to be less than 7%.

Abstract:
The growth kinetics of localized corrosion, e.g. pits, in corrosive environments often controls the service life of metallic components. Yet, our understanding of these kinetics is largely based on coupon-level, e.g. mass-loss, studies which provide limited insights into the evolution of individual damage events. It is critical to relate observed cumulative loss trends, such as links between changing humidity and mass loss rates, to the growth kinetics of individual pits. Towards this goal, we leverage in-situ X-ray computed tomography to measure the growth rates of over sixty pits in aluminum in four different humid, chloride environments over ≈3 days of exposure. Pit growth rates and final volumes increased with increasing droplet volume, which was observed to increase with increasing humidity and salt loading. Two factors, droplet spreading and oxide jacking, dramatically increased pit growth rates and final volumes.

Abstract:
Bare aluminum metal surfaces are highly reactive, which leads to the spontaneous formation of a protective oxide surface layer. Because many subsequent corrosive processes are mediated by water, the structure and dynamics of water at the oxide interface are anticipated to influence corrosion kinetics. Using molecular dynamics simulations with a reactive force field, we model the behavior of aqueous aluminum metal ions in water adsorbed onto aluminum oxide surfaces across a range of ion concentrations and water film thicknesses corresponding to increasing relative humidity. We find that the structure and diffusivity of both the water and the metal ions depend strongly on the humidity of the environment and the relative height within the adsorbed water film. Aqueous aluminum ion diffusion rates in water films corresponding to a typical indoor relative humidity of 30% are found to be more than 2 orders of magnitude slower than self-diffusion of water in the bulk limit. Connections between metal ion diffusivity and corrosion reaction kinetics are assessed parametrically with a reductionist model based on a 1D continuum reaction-diffusion equation. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating the properties specific to interfacial water in predictive models of aluminum corrosion.

Abstract:
All-solid-state lithium batteries (ASSLBs), which use solid electrolytes instead of liquid ones, have become a hot research topic due to their high energy and power density, ability to solve battery safety issues, and capabilities to fulfill the increasing demand for energy storage in electric vehicles and smart grid applications. Garnet-type solid electrolytes have attracted considerable interest as they meet all the properties of an ideal solid electrolyte for ASSLBs. The garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) has excellent environmental stability; experiments and computational analyses showed that this solid electrolyte has a high lithium (Li) ionic conductivity (10−4–10−3 S·cm−1), an electrochemical window as wide as 6 V, stability against Li metal anode, and compatibility with most of the cathode materials. In this review, we present the fundamentals of garnet-type solid electrolytes, preparation methods, air stability, some strategies for improving the conductivity based on experimental and computational results, interfacial issues, and finally applications and challenges for future developments of LLZO solid electrolytes for ASSLBs.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The development of advanced metallic alloys for aerospace applications is continuously progressing to meet new requirements for lightweight construction, energy efficiency, high-temperature operation, durability, and sustainability. The state-of-the-art regarding the most common metallic alloy families currently used in aerospace engineering is presented in this review. These alloys include traditional aluminum alloys, aluminum-lithium alloys, titanium alloys, nickel-based superalloys, and advanced high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The compositions, microstructures, processing methods, potential of additively manufactured parts, mechanical properties, and sustainability characteristics of these alloys were critically evaluated. Third-generation Al-Li alloys provide approximately 2-4% decrease in density and up to 10% increase in stiffness compared to conventional 2xxx and 7xxx aluminum alloys, which makes their use very effective in reducing the weight of structural elements. Titanium alloys still cannot be replaced in aerospace structural applications at medium temperatures, whereas nickel-based superalloys are widely used in turbines operating at temperatures higher than 1100-1200°C. High-entropy alloys demonstrate an outstanding combination of strength, ductility, resistance to corrosion, and high-temperature stability, with several lightweight alloys demonstrating compressive yield strengths higher than 1300 MPa at temperatures close to 1000°C. Additive manufacturing techniques have considerably promoted the adoption of topology-optimized aerospace parts; however, fatigue behavior, qualification, and certification remain problematic issues. Moreover, sustainability concerns, including embodied carbon, recyclability, and lifetime impacts, play a more important role in selecting the optimal alloy. Finally, the gaps in the research regarding long-term fatigue behavior, qualification approaches, manufacturing scalability, and machine learning-based alloy design are discussed and prioritized.</jats:p>

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000007

From text 'ratko2004hydrothermalsynthesisof pages 4-5'.

A. I. Rat'ko, V. E. Romanenkov, E. V. Bolotnikova, and Zh. V. Krupen'kina. Hydrothermal synthesis of porous al2o3/al metal ceramics: i. oxidation of aluminum powder and structure formation of porous al(oh)3/al composite. Kinetics and Catalysis, 45:141-148, Jan 2004. URL: https://doi.org/10.1023/b:kica.0000016114.78885.00, doi:10.1023/b:kica.0000016114.78885.00. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides qualitative mechanistic information relevant to aluminum oxidation and hydroxide formation near ambient conditions, but it does not report a numerical rate law, fitted kinetic constants, activation energies, or a critical relative-humidity threshold. For aluminum powder bearing an amorphous oxide film, oxidation in water follows an S-shaped pH-time curve characteristic of a topochemical process. An induction period involves adsorption of water, hydration of the oxide film, and formation of aluminum-hydroxide island nuclei. Subsequent hydrolysis and access of water to the metal promote hydrogen-producing oxidation and precipitation of hydroxide or pseudoboehmite. The oxide-film structure strongly affects kinetics: crystalline films lack the observed induction period and permit easier initial water access because of interfaces and porosity, although they are more stable toward water than amorphous films. Under vigorous stirring, approximately 50% conversion to hydroxide occurred within the first 3.5 hours, but this condition also promoted transport of soluble aluminum hydroxo complexes away from the particles and reduced deposition on the metal surface. At 25°C and 90% relative humidity, bayerite was detected, along with gibbsite, pseudoboehmite, and traces of γ-Al2O3. Thus, the excerpt demonstrates hydroxide formation at high RH but supplies no data sufficient to establish RH-dependent rate expressions or whether hydration becomes negligible below a defined RH.


---

## pqac-00000008

From text 'czech2010hydrogengenerationfrom pages 23-27'.

Edith Barbara Czech. Hydrogen generation from aluminum-water systems. ArXiv, Jan 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.14288/1.0078738, doi:10.14288/1.0078738. This article has 4 citations.

The excerpt provides qualitative, but not quantitative, information about aluminum oxidation and hydration. Aluminum rapidly forms a protective oxide film: an inert film reaches approximately 10 Å within seconds on freshly exposed metal, while air-formed films are about 2–5 nm thick at room temperature. Film growth is accelerated by increasing temperature and humidity, and immersion in water causes further thickening as the air-formed oxide transforms into gel-like hydroxo-complexes. With aging in aqueous solution, these species transform successively into pseudoboehmite and then bayerite. At temperatures up to 80°C, the predominant products are bayerite and pseudoboehmite; boehmite becomes favored at higher temperatures. The excerpt identifies the Mott–Cabrera framework for passive-film growth, involving outward migration of Al3+ and inward migration of O2−, with metal-cation emission at the metal/oxide interface described as rate limiting. However, it does not provide explicit oxidation rate laws, numerical rate constants, activation energies, powder-specific kinetics, quantitative dependence on relative humidity, or a critical RH threshold below which hydration is negligible. Those requested parameters would require additional experimental or literature sources.


---

## pqac-00000009

From text 'scher2023modelforhumiditymediated pages 33-37'.

Jeremy A. Scher, Stephen E. Weitzner, Yue Hao, Tae Wook Heo, Stephen T. Castonguay, Sylvie Aubry, Susan A. Carroll, and Matthew P. Kroonblawd. Model for humidity-mediated diffusion on aluminum surfaces and its role in accelerating atmospheric aluminum corrosion. ACS applied materials & interfaces, 15:28716-28730, May 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.3c02327, doi:10.1021/acsami.3c02327. This article has 20 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not provide oxidation rate laws, activation energies, or direct kinetic data for aluminum powder oxidation or for boehmite/bayerite formation at 15–50 °C. It instead presents a reductionist 1D diffusion–reaction model for aluminum corrosion pits, constrained by molecular-dynamics-derived Al ion diffusion coefficients. Within the model, corrosion is diffusion-limited across relevant hydrated-film thicknesses and the steady-state reaction rate varies approximately linearly with Al ion diffusivity over the MD-supported range of about 10^-8 to 10^-6 cm2 s^-1. Hydrated alumina surface films strongly suppress Al aqueous-ion transport—by up to approximately a factor of 220 relative to bulk water—and the diffusivity depends strongly on water-film thickness and therefore relative humidity. The excerpt identifies an experimentally observed practical threshold: atmospheric corrosion is not observed on pristine aluminum surfaces below approximately 70% RH, suggesting negligible or strongly suppressed corrosion/hydration there, but it does not establish that hydroxide formation itself is strictly zero below this value. Surface water remains sufficiently confining to reduce ion mobility even at 90% RH. The authors explicitly caution that the model omits detailed reaction chemistry, polarization, participating species, pit geometry, and microstructure, so its results are qualitative and cannot be used to infer phase-specific boehmite or bayerite formation kinetics or activation energies.

Abstract:
Interfacial adhesion between graphene and a SiO2 substrate is studied by density functional theory (DFT) with dispersion corrections. The results demonstrate the van der Waals (vdW) interaction as the predominant mechanism at the graphene/SiO2 interface. It is found that the interaction strength is strongly influenced by changes of the SiO2 surface structures due to surface reactions with water. The adhesion energy is reduced when the reconstructed SiO2 surface is hydroxylated, and further reduced when covered by a monolayer of adsorbed water molecules. Moreover, it is noted that vdW forces are required to accurately model the graphene/SiO2 interface with DFT and that the adhesion energy is underestimated by empirical force fields commonly used in atomistic simulations.

Abstract:
<jats:p>A bilayer tablet formulation approach was used to develop a fixed dose combination tablet formulation of drugs Y & Z. The weight of Layer I containing Drug Y and the weight of Layer II A or II B containing Drug Z were 250 mg and 1280 mg, respectively. While Layer I was manufactured using dry granulation, Layer II A and II B were manufactured using a moisture activated dry granulation (MADG) process. Layer II A and Layer II B contained 3% w/w colloidal silicon dioxide with the surface area of 300 m2/g (Aeroperl® 300) and 200 m2/g (Aerosil® 200), respectively, for moisture scavenging, and otherwise common excipients. Both grades of silicon dioxide were amorphous. When exposed to an open relative humidity of 40°C/75% for 72 hours, the bilayer tablet consisting of Layers I/Layer II A (containing Aeroperl® 300) showed a clear layer separation while the tablet consisting of Layers I/Layer II B (containing Aerosil® 200) did not. If the individual layer is exposed to a similar condition, the projected change in the moisture content for Layer I, Layer II A, and Layer II B, could be 63% w/w, 107% w/w, and 109% w/w, respectively. Thus, the difference in moisture adsorption between Layer I/ Layer II A (containing Aeroperl® 300) than Layer I/Layer II B (containing Aerosil® 200) was similar. The comparison of the moisture adsorption-desorption isotherms for Aeroperl® 300 and Aerosil® 200 suggested that Aeroperl® 300 can adsorb relatively large amounts of moisture at any humidity level due to its greater surface area but it does not retain moisture when the humidity decreases. In contrast, Aerosil 200 adsorb relatively smaller amounts of moisture but it retains moisture due to its larger pore sizes. It is hypothesized that the moisture not retained by Aeroperl® 300 could be available for interaction with other Layer I excipients, such as, microcrystalline cellulose and crospovidone. Such interaction can generate significant shear stress at the layer interface triggering the delamination.</jats:p>

This article has 94 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports progressive surface oxidation of AlSi10Mg powder during prolonged laser powder bed fusion reuse. The initially uniform surface oxide layer, composed of Mg- and Al-based oxides, increased in average thickness from approximately 4 nm for virgin powder to about 38 nm after roughly 30 months of reuse. Aging also produced Mg-base oxide enrichment. Spatter particles developed much thicker columnar oxide scales, reaching approximately 120–125 nm, and their volume fraction increased to as much as 3% after 30 months. The oxide composition was identified as MgAl2O4 spinel and Al2O3 (corundum), based on XPS, STEM-EDX, and thermodynamic calculations. The excerpt indicates that the oxide characteristics were consistent with the measured oxygen content, but it does not provide numerical oxygen-content values. It also does not report hydrogen pickup, storage in humid conditions, or a direct study of moisture effects. Therefore, the provided material supports conclusions about oxide growth, Mg enrichment, spatter oxidation, and oxygen-related degradation during machine reuse, but not quantitative hydrogen absorption or humidity-driven degradation mechanisms.

This article has 65 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt indicates substantial surface oxidation during long-term reuse: the oxide layer thickens from approximately 4 nm on virgin powder to 38 nm on reused powder. Reused powder has more than twice the oxygen content of virgin powder; in the tensile specimens, measured oxygen increased from 0.060 ± 0.017% for virgin powder to 0.070 ± 0.008% for reused powder. The paper attributes aging partly to highly oxidized spatters that remain after sieving and to exposure to residual oxygen and moisture. Powder can absorb oxygen and moisture, and even brief exposure during transfer from the processing station to the glove box can deposit them on particle surfaces. Hydrogen was measured at roughly 80 ppm in virgin powder, while manufactured tensile specimens contained approximately 20 ppm hydrogen for both virgin and reused powders; the specimen values were 0.0022 ± 0.0003% and 0.0020 ± 0.0001%, respectively. Despite the hydrogen surplus, the authors conclude that hydrogen content appears to play only a minor role in pore formation compared with oxide-layer effects. This excerpt does not provide data on Mg enrichment or detailed surface chemistry beyond oxide formation and an oxygen-rich oxide phase in pores. Moisture therefore contributes to degradation by promoting surface contamination and oxide growth, potentially altering laser energy coupling and pore formation.

## pqac-00000018

From text 'asay2006effectsofadsorbed pages 1-3'.

David B. Asay and Seong H. Kim. Effects of adsorbed water layer structure on adhesion force of silicon oxide nanoasperity contact in humid ambient. The Journal of chemical physics, 124 17:174712, May 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1063/1.2192510, doi:10.1063/1.2192510. This article has 300 citations.

The excerpt directly addresses water adsorption on silicon oxide as a function of relative humidity, but the numerical thickness values from Figure 2 are not included in the provided text. It reports that an icelike, structured water layer forms on silicon oxide at room temperature and that both the layer thickness and molecular arrangement change with RH. At lower RH, the infrared spectrum is associated primarily with the approximately 3230 cm−1 OH-stretching peak, attributed to the icelike structure. As RH increases, an approximately 3400 cm−1 peak begins to grow, indicating liquid-like water accumulating on top of the icelike layer. Above roughly 60% RH, the liquid-water peak dominates. Figure 2 is explicitly described as plotting adsorbed-water-layer thickness versus RH, but this excerpt does not provide the graph’s axis values or a conversion into monolayers or angstroms. Therefore, it supports the qualitative trend—initial structured adsorption followed by increasing liquid-like overlayer formation—but not a reliable numerical water coverage or thickness curve. The study used ATR-IR spectroscopy on clean native oxide surfaces under controlled humidity at approximately 22 ± 0.5 °C.

## pqac-00000019

From text 'gao2014interfacialadhesionbetween pages 5-8'.

Wei Gao, Penghao Xiao, Graeme Henkelman, Kenneth M Liechti, and Rui Huang. Interfacial adhesion between graphene and silicon dioxide by density functional theory with van der waals corrections. Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics, 47:255301, May 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/47/25/255301, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/47/25/255301. This article has 201 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt does not provide a quantitative adsorption isotherm relating water coverage or layer thickness to relative humidity. The calculations consider an idealized SiO2 surface with full hydroxylation and one adsorbed water monolayer, rather than varying RH. For that modeled monolayer, the water number density is approximately 9.33 nm^-2. The authors explicitly state that actual silanol density and water adsorption depend on ambient conditions, including relative humidity. Therefore, the excerpt supports only the conclusion that water coverage is RH-dependent and that the modeled case corresponds to a complete monolayer; it does not specify how many monolayers or angstroms of water occur at particular RH values. It also excludes macroscopic capillary effects, which may become important at relatively high humidity. The reported graphene–SiO2 separation with the water monolayer is approximately 5.06 Å, but this is an interface separation, not the thickness of the water film itself, so it should not be interpreted as a direct water-layer thickness.

Physical chemistry chemical physics : PCCP, 16 16:7377-84, Mar 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1039/c3cp54912g, doi:10.1039/c3cp54912g. This article has 56 citations.

The excerpt provides a qualitative, rather than numerical, water-adsorption-versus-relative-humidity relationship for smooth SiO2 plasma-polymer surfaces and SiO2 nanoparticle-coated surfaces. On the nanoparticle-modified SiO2 sample, adsorption is especially rapid from 0–20% RH, where nearly half of the total measured water layer is taken up, consistent with the hydrophilic surface. Between 20% and 80% RH, the isotherm has a relatively low slope and the surface is described as almost saturated. Above approximately 80% RH, adsorption rises sharply because multilayer growth and capillary condensation occur within the particle layer. The particle-coated sample takes up substantially more water than the smooth reference, attributed to capillary water in interparticle and particle–substrate contact regions. A QCM-D surface-area correction factor of approximately 5.3 was applied for the presented nanoparticle dataset, but the excerpt does not report the absolute adsorbed mass, water-film thickness in monolayers, or thickness in angstroms at specific RH values. Therefore, it can establish the RH-dependent regimes and the enhanced uptake caused by nanoparticles, but not a numerical monolayer or Å-versus-RH curve.

The excerpt reports an in situ FT-IRRAS/QCM-D study of water adsorption and capillary-bridge formation in SiO2 nanoparticle layers, but it does not provide a complete numerical water-coverage-versus-relative-humidity curve or a thickness in angstroms. Its key quantitative statement is that approximately two adsorbed water monolayers form on SiO2, while additional uptake is associated with bulk-like water. Up to about 60% relative humidity, the measured dissipation increases rather linearly, consistent with progressive adsorption and the development of the water layer. At higher humidity, capillary liquid bridges form and produce a strong dissipation increase; the excerpt then states that dissipation decreases again when RH is increased to values "490%", which is evidently a formatting/OCR error and likely means approximately 90% RH. The supplied passage therefore supports a qualitative regime description—adsorbed water up to roughly two monolayers, followed by liquid-like/bulk water and capillary condensation—but does not establish a monolayer thickness in Å or precise RH-dependent coverage values. A full answer would require the article’s figures, tables, or supplementary information.

The excerpt identifies approximately 70% relative humidity as the experimentally observed threshold below which atmospheric corrosion does not occur on pristine, clean aluminum surfaces. It therefore supports the conclusion that corrosion is negligible below 70% RH under the conditions discussed, but it does not provide a separate quantitative threshold specifically at 40% RH. The model indicates that humidity affects corrosion through the thickness and transport properties of adsorbed water films: increasing RH changes the surface-water environment and generally increases aqueous aluminum-ion diffusivity, while lower RH produces thinner, more confining films and strongly suppresses ion mobility. Even at 90% RH, surface-water confinement appreciably reduces ion mobility relative to bulk water. For the modeled clean/pristine surface, corrosion kinetics are diffusion limited, and the steady-state reaction rate varies nearly linearly with aluminum-ion diffusivity over the range constrained by molecular dynamics, spanning almost two orders of magnitude. Thus, atmospheric corrosion is expected to increase strongly with humidity rather than remain constant, although the excerpt does not provide a specific corrosion-rate-versus-RH curve or establish a distinct 40% RH cutoff. This article has 94 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt directly addresses magnesium in AlSi10Mg, but it does not provide evidence about lithium, zinc, scandium, cerium, erbium, or copper, nor does it discuss moisture sensitivity specifically. It shows that alloying elements with high oxygen affinity promote oxidation during powder aging and reuse. In AlSi10Mg, surface oxidation develops from an approximately 4 nm oxide layer in virgin powder to about 18 nm after six months and approximately 38 nm after 30 months of reuse. Magnesium plays an important role in the oxide chemistry: it becomes incorporated into the surface oxide and forms MgAl2O4 spinel within the Al2O3-rich layer. Thermodynamic calculations rank MgO as the most stable of the listed oxides, followed by MgAl2O4, Al2O3, and SiO2, although calculations for the alloy composition predict Al2O3, MgAl2O4, and SiO2 rather than MgO under the examined conditions. Spatter particles formed during melting can develop substantially thicker Al- and Mg-containing oxide scales, measured at roughly 50–125 nm, and their increasing fraction contributes to powder degradation. Thus, Mg surface enrichment or Mg participation in the surface oxide increases the complexity and stability of the oxide film and is associated with progressive oxidation during powder reuse.

Abstract:
Abstract Research into new reversible hydrogen storage materials has the potential to help accelerate the transition to a hydrogen economy. The discovery of an efficient and cost‐effective method of safely storing hydrogen would revolutionise its use as a sustainable energy carrier. Accurately measuring storage capacities – particularly of novel nanomaterials – has however proved challenging, and progress is being hindered by ongoing problems with reproducibility. Various metal and complex hydrides are being investigated, together with nanoporous adsorbents such as carbons, metal‐organic frameworks and microporous organic polymers. The hydrogen storage properties of these materials are commonly determined using either the manometric (or Sieverts) technique or gravimetric methods, but both approaches are prone to significant error, if not performed with great care. Although commercial manometric and gravimetric instruments are widely available, they must be operated with an awareness of the limits of their applicability and the error sources inherent to the measurement techniques. This article therefore describes the measurement of hydrogen sorption and covers the required experimental procedures, aspects of troubleshooting and recommended reporting guidelines, with a view of helping improve reproducibility in experimental hydrogen storage material research.

Abstract:
Supersonic cold spraying is an emerging technique for rapid deposition of films of materials including micrometer‐size and sub‐micrometer metal particles, nanoscale ceramic particles, clays, polymers, hybrid materials composed of polymers and particulates, reduced graphene oxide (rGO), and metal–organic frameworks. In this method, particles are accelerated to a high velocity and then impact a substrate at near ambient temperature, where dissipation of their kinetic energy produces strong adhesion. Here, recent progress in fundamentals and applications of cold spraying is reviewed. High‐velocity impact with the substrate results in significant deformation, which not only produces adhesion, but can change the particles' internal structure. Cold‐sprayed coatings can also exhibit micro‐ and nanotextured morphologies not achievable by other means. Suspending micro‐ or nanoparticles in a liquid and cold‐spraying the suspension produces fine atomization and even deposition of materials that could not otherwise be processed. The scalability and low cost of this method and its compatibility with roll‐to‐roll processing make it promising for many applications, including ultrathin flexible materials, solar cells, touch‐screen panels, nanotextured surfaces for enhanced heat transfer, thermal and electrical insulation films, transparent conductive films, materials for energy storage (e.g., Li‐ion battery electrodes), heaters, sensors, photoelectrodes for water splitting, water purification membranes, and self‐cleaning films.

Abstract:
Mg2TMHn complex hydrides, where TM represents various combinations of transition metals, were synthesized by reactive ball milling of Mg and TM powders under H2 pressure. TM was an equimolar mixture of three (Fe, Co, and Ni), four (Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni), or five (Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni) elements. The Mg/TM ratio was either 2:1 or 3:1. For 2:1 samples, a single fcc hydride phase Mg2TMHn with a K2PtCl6-type structure was detected by X-ray diffraction along with a residual, unreacted metal phase. By contrast, in samples where the Mg/TM ratio was 3:1, the tetragonal MgH2 hydride was also observed. The formation of Mg3TMHn complex hydrides, previously reported for TM = Cr and Mn under high-pressure conditions, was not detected. The maximum hydrogen content in the as-milled state was about 5 wt% for samples with a 3:1 Mg/TM ratio as determined by temperature-programmed desorption. The as-milled hydrides exhibited similar onset temperatures for desorption independently of the TM composition, suggesting no destabilization induced by elements like Mn and Cr that are known to form only unstable, high-pressure hydrides. The reversible hydrogen storage, investigated by pressure–composition isotherms in a Sieverts-type apparatus, arises from both the Mg-MgH2 and the Mg2TM-Mg2TMHn transformations. Within the 0.1–20 bar and 285–320 °C window, the samples with a 3:1 Mg/TM ratio exhibit a reversible gravimetric capacity in the 3.7–4.2 wt% range depending on TM composition, while those with a 2:1 ratio are in the 3.0–3.2 wt% range. The decreased reversible capacity compared to the initial hydrogen content was associated with the phase segregation of the transition metals, particularly Cr and Mn, which was highlighted by X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy with nanoscale microanalysis.

## pqac-00000032

From text 'kim2025investigationofmicrostructure pages 3-6'.

H. Kim, S. Jo, I.-S. Kim, and S.-J. Hong. Investigation of microstructure and mechanical properties of sts 316l powder according to humidity in the ded process. Journal of the Japan Society of Powder and Powder Metallurgy, 72:S1459-S1464, Mar 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.2497/jjspm.16p-t6-09, doi:10.2497/jjspm.16p-t6-09. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt provides evidence that STS 316L powder is sensitive to humidity under the tested storage conditions. Samples were exposed for 24 hours to dry conditions and relative humidities of 5%, 35%, 50%, and 70%. Increasing humidity produced higher moisture uptake and increased oxygen and hydrogen contents, indicating that humid storage promotes moisture absorption and surface oxidation-related changes. The powder also became less cohesive-flowable: Hall Flowmeter results showed progressively poorer flow, with the highest-humidity Sample E becoming completely non-flowing and unsuitable for DED according to the stated specifications. Rotating-drum and RPA measurements similarly showed reduced flowability with increasing humidity. However, the excerpt does not report the precise storage temperature, oxidation rates, or a controlled comparison involving a 2–5°C temperature change or a 20% RH change. Therefore, it cannot establish whether stainless-steel oxidation at 20–30°C is more strongly affected by either of those specific changes. It also contains no information about silicon powder oxidation at room temperature. The study’s direct conclusion is limited to the relationship between humidity exposure, increased moisture/oxygen content, and powder flowability in 316L.
